clue.text: Roughly object to acquiring computer language

parts.note: c. for circa, Latin for about or roughly

indicators.note: to acquire something is to take it in, so one piece ends up held inside another

parts.note: to object to something is to resent it
C is a well-known programming language

explanation.surface: Someone grumpily complains about having to learn a programming language.
explanation.walkthrough: This is one of the eight theme answers, so there is no definition: it pairs with MORNINGTON for Mornington Crescent, a game on the BBC radio panel show I'm Sorry I Haven't a Clue.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition is given; the preamble explains that the thematic entries are clued by wordplay only.

clue.text: Wish one could be like diplomat missing nothing

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so a letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: an envoy is a diplomatic representative
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A young person dreams of becoming a diplomat but lacks the means.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the O from ENVOY leaves ENVY.
explanation.definitionFit: To envy someone is to covet their position, wishing their circumstances were your own.

clue.text: Dog taken over police station without lead

indicators.note: taking something over can mean wrapping round it, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: a pup is a young dog

indicators.note: the lead is the front, so going without it means losing the opening letter

parts.note: nick is British slang for a police station; it loses its first letter

explanation.surface: A dog is walked into a police station off its leash.
explanation.walkthrough: A theme answer with no definition: it pairs with SONG for Pick-up Song, a round on I'm Sorry I Haven't a Clue. 'Without lead' sounds like the dog's leash but strips the first letter of NICK.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition is given; the preamble explains that the thematic entries are clued by wordplay only.

clue.text: Express enthusiasm, not ecstasy, holding tot up

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece sits within another
saying not before a thing removes it from what precedes

parts.note: to cheer is to show enthusiasm
E is slang for the drug ecstasy; one E leaves the cheer

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to tot up is to add

explanation.surface: A cheerleader stays off drugs while lifting a toddler aloft.
explanation.walkthrough: A theme answer with no definition: it pairs with GORGE for Cheddar Gorge, a game on I'm Sorry I Haven't a Clue. 'Tot' looks like a toddler but means add, written backwards inside CHER.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition is given; the preamble explains that the thematic entries are clued by wordplay only.

clue.text: Clothes an American soldier's given up to saint

indicators.note: in a down entry, sending letters up means they read from the bottom, so their order flips

parts.note: a suit is a set of clothes
taken as written
GI is the usual term for a US soldier

explanation.surface: A GI donates his uniform to a holy man.
explanation.walkthrough: The three pieces join as SUITANGI and then the whole string is read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, is one of several canonised Christians bearing that name.

clue.text: Pressure on an emperor to move — one should take a capital

parts.note: P is the symbol for pressure

indicators.note: moving things around changes their positions, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Political pressure is put on an emperor to relocate to a new seat of government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' suggests a city, as the emperor scene invites, but here it means a capital letter. In a down clue, P 'on' the rest means P sits above it.
explanation.definitionFit: Names of specific people and places are written with an initial upper-case letter in English.

clue.text: Notice about liberation movement's spirited meeting

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the outside of another

parts.note: to see is to notice
the African National Congress, South Africa's liberation movement

explanation.surface: A poster announces a lively rally of a freedom movement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirited' suggests a lively meeting, but it is one involving spirits of the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: A séance is a gathering where participants try to contact ghosts, so it is literally full of spirits.

clue.text: Prominently display constipation cure?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to wave something about for all to see
second meaning, split in two: a bowl of high-fibre cereal husks

explanation.surface: A laxative remedy is showcased in an advert.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful split into BRAN DISH; bran is the fibrous husk of grain, a traditional remedy for constipation.
explanation.definitionFit: To brandish a weapon or object is to flourish it showily so that everyone notices.

clue.text: Shed blood that's good to drink

indicators.note: drinking takes something inside, so one piece swallows another

parts.note: gore is spilt blood
G is the standard abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A vampire approves of spilt blood as a beverage.
explanation.walkthrough: A theme answer with no definition: it pairs with CHEDDAR for Cheddar Gorge, a game on I'm Sorry I Haven't a Clue.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition is given; the preamble explains that the thematic entries are clued by wordplay only.

clue.text: Very pale coconuts here

definitions.note: read as 'a shy', a noun phrase
definitions.meaning: second meaning, split in two: a fairground stall where coconuts are knocked down

explanation.surface: Coconut flesh is described as very pale.
explanation.walkthrough: A coconut shy is a British fairground game where you throw balls to knock coconuts off stands, so 'coconuts here' is A SHY.
explanation.definitionFit: An ashy complexion is greyish and drained of colour, like the powder left after burning.

clue.text: Does it suggest teacher is boring? That's criminal conduct

definitions.text: Does it suggest teacher is boring?
definitions.meaning: cryptic meaning, split in two: a child dozing in class
straight meaning: the crime of abducting a person

explanation.surface: A sleepy pupil hints that lessons are dull, which is practically a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as KID NAPPING, the word paints a child asleep at the desk, which suggests the teacher is boring.
explanation.definitionFit: Abducting and holding someone against their will is a serious offence under the law.

clue.text: Storm brewing in it?

parts.note: surface reading: bad weather building up
setter's reading: a fuss over nothing happens in a small china vessel, and brewing is what the drink does

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'a storm in a teacup' means a big fuss over a trivial matter; 'brewing' doubles as what happens to tea.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverbial location of a trivial fuss is the small cup used for drinking the hot beverage.

clue.text: Lose nerve and smart, energy being put into whip

parts.note: chic means stylish or smart

indicators.note: putting one thing into another places it inside

parts.note: a knout is a Russian whip
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A coward flinches as the sting of a whip lash lands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart' looks like the sting of the whip but means stylish. A knout is an old Russian whip; E slips in after its K.
explanation.definitionFit: To chicken out is an informal idiom for backing down through fear at the last moment.

clue.text: A sign on six cages

indicators.note: in an across entry, one thing placed on another is written after it, so the order follows that

parts.note: taken as written
VI is six in Roman numerals
Aries is a sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: A notice is fixed onto six animal enclosures.
explanation.walkthrough: Aries, the ram, is one of the twelve zodiac signs; the clue lists it before the numeral but it is written after.
explanation.definitionFit: Aviaries are large enclosures for keeping birds, a particular kind of cage.

clue.text: Tour changed to skirt bad street artist

indicators.note: to skirt is to go around the edge, so one piece encircles another
something changed is altered, so the letters take a new order

parts.note: letters to be rearranged
ill means bad, as in ill effects

explanation.surface: A rerouted tour detours around a rough neighbourhood's busker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Street artist' suggests graffiti or busking, but Maurice Utrillo was a French painter famous for Montmartre street scenes.
explanation.definitionFit: Utrillo painted mostly Parisian townscapes, the lanes and squares of Montmartre, so he was literally a painter of streets.

clue.text: Drink number one taken in shelter

indicators.note: something taken in is admitted inside, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: lee is shelter from the wind
a monad is a unit, the number one in philosophy

explanation.surface: A drinker downs a first round in a bus shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number one' is not a digit but MONAD, a word for a single unit.
explanation.definitionFit: Lemonade is a sweet citrus soft beverage, an example of something you drink.

clue.text: Invite to tango, bumping daughter sideways

parts.note: to ask someone is to invite them

indicators.note: to bump someone is to knock them out of place, so a letter is ejected

parts.note: to tango is to dance
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A man asks a woman to tango, jostling her daughter aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sideways' is an adverb, matching how the word is used in the phrase 'look askance'; 'bumping' suggests a crowded dance floor but only knocks out a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To look askance is to glance obliquely, often with suspicion, out of the corner of the eye.

clue.text: Hard case needs resolution

indicators.note: resolving a puzzle means sorting out its parts, so the letters are reorganised

parts.note: letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A difficult court case is waiting to be settled.

clue.text: Get this to go away — it's complicated

definitions.meaning: first meaning: completes a rude British brush-off telling someone to clear off
second meaning: tangled up in tight loops

explanation.surface: Someone is told to leave because things have become too messy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get knotted!' is a mildly rude British phrase meaning go away or get lost.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangled rope or a tangled situation is twisted and intricate, hard to unravel.

clue.text: After a month, relative drops in — he's on target

indicators.note: coming after places the second piece behind the first

parts.note: Mar is the short form of March

indicators.note: to drop something is to let it go, so letters are removed

parts.note: a kinsman is a male relative
taken as written, the letters removed

explanation.surface: A month later, a relative pays a visit and is right on schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drops in' reads as visiting, but it means KINSMAN loses the letters IN.
explanation.definitionFit: A marksman is a skilled shooter, someone whose shots hit the bullseye.

clue.text: Stir Up Sunday passed over by a lecher

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down entry, being passed over means having something above and around, so one piece is enveloped

parts.note: a roué is a debauched man
S is short for Sunday

explanation.surface: Stir-up Sunday, the British day for mixing Christmas puddings, is skipped by a lecherous man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stir Up Sunday' looks like one name, but the definition is 'Stir Up' and Sunday is just S.
explanation.definitionFit: To arouse feelings or a crowd is to excite or provoke them, like whipping them into action.

clue.text: A salad for vocal exponent of 11

definitions.note: the salad named for him, a Caesar salad

indicators.note: vocal means spoken, so the word is to be heard rather than read

parts.note: a practitioner of the crime at 11-across is someone who seizes people

explanation.surface: A salad recipe is offered to a kidnapper with a loud voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 is KIDNAPPING, whose exponent is a seizer; a Caesar salad is a familiar dish of romaine and croutons.
explanation.definitionFit: The well-known lettuce dish takes its name from the Roman ruler's name, giving a salad called after it.

clue.text: Is wild animal able to bite?

parts.note: to be able is can
an ape is a wild animal

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a wild creature is capable of biting.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's question form is the trick: asking whether something is able is turning 'can' to the front. 'Bite' looks like a verb but is a noun for a mouthful.
explanation.definitionFit: A canapé is a small savoury snack served at parties, a single mouthful of food.

clue.text: Poetically, east to north

parts.note: in poetry the east, where the sun rises, is the morning
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for north

clue.text: Now settled, but exhausted

definitions.meaning: first meaning: paid out, so no longer pending

explanation.walkthrough: 'Now settled' reads as calm, but it means a bill that has been paid, its money spent.
explanation.definitionFit: Resources that are spent are used up completely, the same as being drained or depleted.
